item.title: Lauren Goodlad, "Teaching Critical AI Literacies" — Wed Sep 23, 4:30 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
Since the release of ChatGPT in November 2022, classrooms and learning platforms the world over have been inundated with generative AI (gen AI) in ways that burden educators while posing serious harm to student learning and critical skills. At many institutions, the documented harms of the technology are overlooked in favor of an uncritical push for vaguely defined standards of "AI literacy" and "AI competency"-with little or no consultation with faculty or attention to the desired course objectives or learning goals. The industry-driven push to adopt "AI first and fast" disempowers faculty and students alike. Occasionally institutional decision-makers pay lip-service to harms while devoting scarce resources to "FOMO" and keeping up with Joneses.

item.title: Prescribing Art? — Wed Sep 23, 6:00 PM — Rubenstein Arts Center
item.description:
Chris Appleton of Social Rx and Dr. Anne Basting of TimeSlips join Prof. Sarah Wilbur to look at the past and future of arts-based referral practices and their nationwide expansion.
This is the first of a three-part public conversation series bringing together arts, humanities, medicine and healthcare professionals, artists, community leaders, and students from Duke and Durham to explore how creative practices can support healing, connection, and wellbeing. From national, state, and local efforts to prescribe arts engagement for wellbeing, to emerging policy platforms and workforce development, each event hosts two handpicked leaders from arts and health professions to share work and insights.
This series is moderated by Dr. Sarah Wilbur, dance-and-health practitioner and arts-labor researcher (Dance & Theater Studies).
Free and open to the public! Please RSVP at link below.

item.title: Duke Arts at American Tobacco: Ken Pomeroy — Wed Sep 23, 6:30 PM — American Tobacco Campus - Lawn
item.description:
Cherokee songwriter Ken Pomeroy writes songs that cut straight to the heart. Her music pairs a soft soprano with spare guitar and clear-eyed storytelling, creating songs that feel both fragile and powerful.
Raised in Moore, Oklahoma, Pomeroy began writing at age eleven and quickly developed a reputation for lyrics that carry unusual emotional weight. Her music has appeared on the Twisters film soundtrack and in the acclaimed series Reservation Dogs, bringing her work to a growing national audience.
Pomeroy is emerging as a striking new voice in roots music, drawing from personal experience and Native storytelling traditions to shape songs that linger.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Dynamic Individuals, Static Neighborhoods: Migration and Earnings Changes in Poor Neighborhoods — Thu Sep 24, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description:
This paper studies migration and earnings dynamics in poor neighborhoods using new administrative data linking residential location and earnings. Out-migration rates are higher in poor neighborhoods than elsewhere, and the majority of people who leave a poor neighborhood move to a richer one. Residents of poor neighborhoods also see significant earnings mobility, with average growth rates similar to richer areas. Estimates based on idiosyncratic, firm-specific pay changes show that increases in earnings are linked to migration to better neighborhoods. This results in the earnings of the cohort who lived in a poor neighborhood at baseline growing more than twice as fast as the earnings of these neighborhoods' contemporaneous residents. Overall, our results highlight an underappreciated reason why poor neighborhoods stay poor: initial residents whose earnings grow tend to move away.
Source: Duke University

Dr. Efrén Pérez (UCLA) will present his talk, "Taking Stock of Solidarity Between People of Color in U.S. Politics: Assimilated Evidence, New Challenges, and Fresh Opportunities."
Abstract: Recent work suggests that solidarity between people of color (PoC) is triggered when a racially stigmatized ingroup believes they are discriminated similarly to another outgroup based on their alleged foreigness or inferiority. Heightened solidarity is then supposed to boost support for policies that benefit racially stigmatized outgroups who are not one's own-for example, Black adults become more pro-Latino, Asian adults become more pro-Black, and Latino adults become more pro-Asian. In this talk, I discuss my lab's growing experimental evidence on this proposed mechanism. I then highlight new challenges and opportunities to learn more-both theoretically and methodologically-about interminority solidarity in politics. item.title: Mixed-Media Floral Greeting Cards — Fri Oct 30, 10:00 AM — Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center
item.description: In this guided mixed-media workshop with Patricia Efunsade, founder and creative director of SaKredJoi Art, participants will create a series of botanically inspired greeting cards using a simple and approachable collage process. Begin by creating an 8.5 x 11-inch collage master sheet—a mixed-media process rooted in experimentation, layering, composition and storytelling through paper. Participants will then transform the paper into four unique handmade cards with designs that feature hand-cut flowers, stems and leaves. Everyone will complete four finished greeting cards, with the option to add personal words or sentiments. This workshop is designed to be both relaxing and creatively engaging, with a clear process that allows participants of all experience levels to leave with finished work that is ready to send or frame.
